source_identity.canonical_title: La misandrie est une réponse à la misogynie et se veut majoritairement non violente

translation.canonical_title: Misandry is a response to misogyny and is intended to be predominantly nonviolent
translation.displayed_title: Misandry is a response to misogyny and is intended to be predominantly nonviolent
translation.summary:
Openly expressed misandry, whether conveyed through hashtags such as #menaretrash or #balancetonporc, makes men bristle, and they readily respond with #notallmen or “not all men are monsters.” Granted. Women do attack, admittedly in an apparently stigmatizing form, but this comes after millennia of patriarchy and just as many platforms calling their legitimacy into question. So many burned bras and angry bare breasts displaying feminist slogans, only to be accused yet again of inherently hating men. It is not that simple. Unlike misogyny, misandry is not institutionalized, is nonviolent (few victims to date), and is intended as a direct response to masculinism and a sexist literary tradition. By that reckoning, potential future centuries of literary misandry would not erase all the misogynistic writings of past centuries. At worst, men risk seeing some women voluntarily turn away from heterosexuality, as Virginie Despentes did, or being ignored. If a misandrist movement exists, its momentum remains negligible compared with existing patriarchal foundations, and its lethal risks are minor. If we nostalgically remember the Spice Girls’ #girlpower, it must be recognized that no female group or collective anywhere on Earth claims THE power, or indeed any power over men. The context of the “misandrist” writings and statements of certain zealous feminists must be restored: they always arise in a context in which men act as predators. And the figures support those feminists’ position. In an article in Libération published after the release of her book I Hate Men, Pauline Harmange discusses the insults and threats that followed. Like her, those who dare to brave the prospect of sexuality without men or who attack masculinity face a machine designed to discredit them, and are readily equated with hairy, masculinized, sexually frustrated truck drivers. It is well known: if THE woman shouts, she is a poorly penetrated old maid. One thinks of Milla, a young queer woman threatened with death on social media following her invectives against Islam and her coming out; of Simone Veil entering the chamber amid antisemitic and sexist insults while defending the right to abortion; and of Dominique Bombardier, who came to denounce pedophilia and proclaim her disgust with Gabriel Matzneff on Pivot’s television program, only to be called a “slut” and “sexually frustrated” afterward...
We observe that some men and elites react very violently when they feel their prerogatives are threatened. Let us not forget that “hating” a man in so-called “modern” feminism primarily means:
- reinventing female sexuality to escape the dictates of invasive male penetration
- fighting a conformist image of passive women
- defending oneself in order to reject rape, assault and sexism
- emancipating oneself in all areas toward equality with men
- fighting the institution of patriarchy rather than men themselves We will conclude by agreeing with these gentlemen: yes, some women are violent, some behave badly after a divorce, some struggle to express their fear of men, others will invariably play the sexism card in their defense, some remain vindictive even toward one another, and some women are capable of the worst... yes, yes and yes. But many, if not the majority, merely want a little empathy.

Détester les hommes et tout ce qu'ils représentent est notre droit le plus strict. C'est aussi une fête. Qui aurait cru qu'il y aurait autant de joie dans la misandrie

Our misandry frightens men because it is a sign that they will have to begin earning our attention.
Hating men and everything they represent is our absolute right. It is also a celebration. Who would have thought there could be so much joy in misandry?
